items.prompt: Which writing system is used in this example?

choices.rationale: Yes. The curved kana さ・く・ら form the word さくら.
Katakana has different, often angular character shapes.
Kanji are character forms such as 山 and 日.

items.explanation: さくら is written in hiragana. Both hiragana and katakana represent Japanese sound units, but they use different character shapes.

items.prompt: Which writing system is used in this example?

choices.rationale: This word uses angular katakana, not rounded hiragana.
Yes. コーヒー is a borrowed word written in katakana.
Kanji are different characters used for many word roots and meanings.

items.explanation: コーヒー (coffee) is a common loanword written in katakana. The long-vowel mark ー is also visible.

items.prompt: Which writing system is used in this example?

choices.rationale: Yes. 山 is a kanji that can mean mountain.
Romaji would show a word with Latin letters, like yama.
This is the kanji 山, not a katakana character.

items.explanation: 山 is kanji, read やま in this example. Kanji can have multiple readings in other words.

items.prompt: What do we call Japanese represented in Latin letters?

choices.rationale: Correct. Romaji uses Latin letters to represent Japanese sounds.
Hiragana would be さくら, using Japanese kana.
Furigana are reading hints, usually small kana above or beside kanji.

items.explanation: “sakura” uses Latin letters, so it is romaji; the word can be written さくら in hiragana.

items.prompt: Which statement about katakana is most accurate?

choices.text: It is commonly used for loanwords and sometimes for emphasis.
choices.rationale: Correct. Katakana has several uses, including loanwords and emphasis.

choices.text: It is a separate spoken language from Japanese.
choices.rationale: Both kana scripts are used to write Japanese.

choices.text: It always shows the English spelling of a word.
choices.rationale: Borrowed words adapt to Japanese sounds and writing conventions.

items.explanation: Katakana often writes loanwords, but also occurs with names, sounds, emphasis, and other functions.

items.prompt: Can a single normal Japanese sentence combine hiragana, katakana, and kanji?

choices.text: Yes, these scripts often appear together.
choices.rationale: Correct. Japanese normally uses multiple scripts together where appropriate.

choices.text: No, writers must choose only one script per sentence.
choices.rationale: The lesson shows that script mixing is normal.

choices.text: Only when translating an English sentence.
choices.rationale: This is ordinary Japanese orthography, not just translation.

items.explanation: A sentence such as 私はコーヒーを飲みます。 mixes kanji, katakana and hiragana naturally.

items.prompt: Where does a verb often appear in a basic Japanese sentence?

choices.text: Near the end of the sentence.
choices.rationale: Right. This is a helpful initial observation, not an absolute grammar rule.

choices.text: Always between the subject and object, as in English.
choices.rationale: English and Japanese often have different basic word orders.
This is not a normal rule of Japanese sentence structure.

items.explanation: Japanese frequently places the verb at the end, as in わたしはおちゃをのみます。 Word order has exceptions and context matters.

choices.rationale: Correct. Furigana help readers pronounce written kanji words.

choices.text: A fourth full Japanese writing system.
choices.rationale: Furigana are reading aids, usually written using kana.
That is romaji.

items.explanation: Furigana use small kana to show readings; they are not a separate primary Japanese writing system.
